metadata.title: AI's Four Chips.
metadata.note: Standalone teaching explainer (~3min) on AI specialized compute: CPU, GPU, TPU, NPU. FRAMEWORK-FIRST (built to pass PROOF): the lens is shown before any example (B01: AI = parallel matrix math), then the four chips (B02), the general↔specialized spectrum/rubric (B03), a worked example (B04: phone face-unlock → NPU), a falsifiability/edge case (B05: it's a division of labor, not a ranking), then a scaffolded task (B07). ONE insight: AI is mostly parallel matrix math, so chips trade generality for AI-specific speed along a spectrum; match the chip to the job. DOUBLE-CHECK LAW: no benchmarks, model names, or version numbers; chip roles described generically (CPU generalist; GPU many parallel cores; TPU custom tensor silicon; NPU low-power on-device). Bookends render (composer/verdict/handoff/outro via Claude Remotion comps); body B01-B05 are house-style 4K PIL cards generated by make_cards.py.

beats.narration_text: Hey, I'm Muskan. CPU, GPU, TPU, NPU, it's alphabet soup. But there's a simple idea underneath. AI does mostly one kind of math, and these chips are just different bets on how to do it fast. Let me give you a lens that makes all four make sense.

props.command: CPU, GPU, TPU, NPU — what's the actual difference, and why does AI need special chips?
output: AI = mostly one kind of math
match the chip to the job

beats.narration_text: Start with the workload. Normal computing is a few complex steps, done in order, that's what a CPU is great at. But AI is different: it's billions of tiny multiply-and-adds, the same simple math, over and over. To be fast, you don't want one clever core, you want to do enormous amounts of it at once. That's the whole story: AI is parallel matrix math.

show.event: left column: a few steps, in order
right column: the same math, all at once (accent)

card.title: Why Special Chips?
card.subtitle: the AI workload
card.caption: AI is mostly one thing: huge amounts of parallel matrix math
card.footer: GENERAL = STEPS IN ORDER · AI = THE SAME MATH, IN PARALLEL

beats.narration_text: So here are the four. A CPU has a few powerful cores and runs everything. A GPU has thousands of simpler cores, built for parallel math, it's the workhorse of AI. A TPU is a custom chip built specifically for tensor math. And an NPU is a small, low-power one that runs AI right on your device.

card.title: Four Kinds of Chip.
card.subtitle: same job, handled differently

items.quote: a few powerful cores · runs everything

card.caption: the same job — matrix math — with very different trade-offs

beats.narration_text: Line them up and you get a spectrum, from general to specialized. The CPU does anything. The GPU is faster at AI but less flexible. The TPU and NPU are faster still, but they only do a narrow job. The rule: the more specialized the chip, the more AI speed you get, and the less it can do anything else.

show.event: the axis draws, general on the left
the four markers land left to right

card.title: One Spectrum.
card.subtitle: general ↔ specialized
card.caption: the more specialized the chip, the more AI speed — and the less it can do anything else

beats.narration_text: Watch the lens pick a chip. You unlock your phone with your face. That's a small AI job that has to be instant, private, and work with no signal. So it doesn't go to a giant GPU in the cloud, it runs on the NPU, right there in your phone, in milliseconds. Small job, on-device, low power, that's the NPU's whole reason to exist.

show.event: the face + question feed the chip
the answer resolves on the NPU (accent)

card.title: One Task, One Chip.
card.subtitle: unlocking your phone
card.answer: a small neural net, on-device → match in milliseconds · no cloud
card.caption: instant, private, works offline — so it runs on the NPU, not a cloud GPU
card.footer: SMALL JOB · ON-DEVICE · LOW POWER → NPU

beats.narration_text: Now the trap. This is not a ranking, newer doesn't mean better. A TPU can't run your operating system. An NPU won't train a big model. And a CPU still runs the whole show and hands the heavy math off. It's a division of labor, not a leaderboard, you match the chip to the job.

show.event: the myth column vs the reality column build

card.title: Not a Ranking.
card.subtitle: a division of labor
right_flow: a TPU can't run your OS
the CPU still runs it all
card.caption: specialization buys speed at the cost of flexibility — you still need all of them

beats.narration_text: So, the lens: AI is parallel matrix math, and each chip is a different trade between general and specialized. CPU runs everything, GPU is the AI workhorse, TPU and NPU go all-in on speed. Match the chip to the job.

artifactLines: The AI workload is massive parallel matrix math — that's why a general CPU alone isn't enough.
CPU = generalist (runs everything); GPU = thousands of cores for parallel math (the workhorse).
TPU = custom silicon built for tensors; NPU = low-power AI on your device (phone / laptop).
It's a spectrum, general → specialized: more speed, less flexibility. Match the chip to the job — not a ranking.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Look at the device you're on right now. Does it have an NPU or an AI chip? Then ask: which AI features run on the device, and which ones call the cloud, and why would each one live where it does? That question is this whole video, applied to your own hardware.
